title: In a dry land (Psalm 63)
hook: my soul thirsts for you in a dry and weary land

segments.voice: Yesterday, my soul waits: a soul that goes quiet toward God. Your line was in silence, waiting. Did you let one small gap stay empty? Day four hundred twenty-six.

East of Jerusalem the land falls away fast. Within an hour's walk the green is gone, and the hills turn the color of bread crust, folding down toward the Dead Sea, one of the lowest places on earth. Shade is a rock's width. Water is a rumor. This is the wilderness of Judah, where shepherds have always known exactly how far it is to the next spring. The heading of Psalm sixty-three puts David here, on the run. Which time is a fair question. He fled into that wilderness from King Saul, and years later from his own son. Either way, a man with a crown or a claim to one is out in the dust, and his throat is dry.
screen: `EAST OF JERUSALEM.` → `THE WILDERNESS OF JUDAH.` → `A KING ON THE RUN.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible the psalm begins: "O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is." Here's what the English hides. The Hebrew word for soul is nephesh. It means life, self, a living being. But it can also mean the throat, the neck, the place where breath and water go in. So when David says my soul thirsteth, a Hebrew listener could also hear: my throat is parched. The body and the longing are one word. He isn't using thirst as a pretty metaphor for a spiritual feeling. He is genuinely thirsty, and he notices that what he wants most is God. Then the psalm does something unexpected for a man in a desert. It praises. "Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee." Better than life. Better than water, then, in a place where water is life. And it moves from dawn to night. "Early will I seek thee," it says at the start, and later, "When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches." He lies awake in the dark, in a dry land, and remembers. Because of that word early, churches have prayed this psalm at the start of the day for many centuries. In the Orthodox morning service it's one of six psalms read in the half-dark, and in the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours it opens Sunday morning prayer. A desert psalm, prayed over coffee.
screen: `A DRY AND THIRSTY LAND` · `NEPHESH: SOUL, AND THROAT` · `BETTER THAN LIFE` · `A DESERT PSALM FOR EARLY MORNING` · then, large: `MY SOUL THIRSTETH FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drink a glass of water slowly. If you can, pour one now. Hold it a moment. Notice the weight, the cold, the light in it. Take one small sip, and feel it all the way down your throat, the place the Hebrew calls nephesh. Then another. Don't hurry. Let your body tell you how much it wanted this. If you pray, you can let each sip carry the psalm's first words: O God, thou art my God. If you don't, just be thirsty, and be met. The bell holds the time.
In a dry land. Psalm sixty-three: David in the wilderness of Judah, with a dry throat and a soul thirsting for God.
Your line: thirsty for God. Today, every time you drink something, take the first sip slowly, and notice what else in you is thirsty. Day four hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Psalm 63 is a traditional morning psalm: Orthodox Christians read it among the six psalms at the start of Matins, and Catholics pray it at Sunday Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

original.note: Hebrew: soul, life, self, and also the throat. "my soul thirsteth" can be heard as "my throat is dry".

trapdoor: what you thought: thirsting for God is a nice spiritual metaphor.
what it means: a man in a real desert, really thirsty, noticing that what he wants most is God.
what a scholar hears: nephesh, soul, also means throat, so body and longing are one word; and the heading's 'wilderness of Judah' fits either Saul's pursuit or Absalom's revolt.

notes: Nephesh as 'throat/neck' is a standard lexical sense (e.g. Isaiah 5:14; Jonah 2:5). Confirm phrasing.
Which flight the heading refers to (from Saul, 1 Samuel 23–24, or from Absalom, 2 Samuel 15) is debated; script leaves it open.

Liturgical claims: Psalm 63 (LXX 62) is one of the Six Psalms (Hexapsalmos: 3, 38, 63, 88, 103, 143) at Orthodox Matins; in the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is the first psalm of Sunday Morning Prayer, Week I. Confirm.
Dead Sea described as 'one of the lowest places on earth' (it is the lowest land elevation). Confirm.
